about: Tools for training a code language model, grouped by workflow role. Versions and dates come from the PyPI JSON API or the GitHub releases API on the check date; install lines come from each project's own README or docs.
notes: Training frameworks pin different dependency versions (Axolotl pins transformers==5.20.1 and trl==1.14.1, LLaMA-Factory caps datasets<=4.0.0, OpenRLHF pins deepspeed==0.19.6). Give each framework its own virtual environment.

Python floors on 2026-11-25: transformers, TRL, PEFT, Accelerate, vLLM and SGLang need 3.11 or newer; datasets 3.10; EvalPlus 3.9; Axolotl, SkyRL, Harbor and text-dedup 3.12. The macOS system Python 3.9.6 is too old for the training stack.

Sandboxes differ in what they isolate. Docker, nsjail and Apptainer use the host kernel; gVisor intercepts system calls; Firecracker, and E2B per its docs, use virtual machines; Modal offers gVisor or a VM runtime. SandboxFusion documents no isolation strength.

roles.title: Collection
roles.summary: Get source files, metadata and events with known provenance: clones and API scripts, Software Heritage, streamed Hub datasets, GH Archive, BigCode's scripts.

roles.title: Processing
roles.summary: Filter, deduplicate, parse, scan for secrets, personal data and licenses, and reshape records.

roles.title: Tokenization
roles.summary: Turn text into token ids with the same tokenizer and special tokens the model uses, including fill-in-the-middle markers.

roles.title: Training and sampling
roles.summary: Fine-tune or RL-train a model, and the engines that sample from it during RL and evaluation.

roles.title: Tracking and artifacts
roles.summary: Log metrics and configs for each run and store versioned checkpoints and datasets.

roles.title: Execution
roles.summary: Run generated code in isolation for tests, rewards and evaluation; the isolation each tool documents is stated in its entry.

roles.title: Evaluation
roles.summary: Score a model with execution-based benchmarks and agentic task suites.

tools.name: git clone and GitHub REST API scripts

latest_release.note: git and the REST API are services, not versioned packages

tools.what: Lists public repositories through the GitHub REST API and fetches each one with git clone, so you control which repositories, branches and commits enter the corpus.
tools.when: Reach for it when you need a small, well-documented repository set with exact commit hashes; for millions of repositories use Software Heritage, because the API enforces primary rate limits.
tools.connects: Takes a repository list or search query and hands cloned working trees (with commit SHAs and license files) to the processing step.
tools.evidence: Read the GitHub Docs page on REST API rate limits (primary limit depends on authentication method) on 2026-11-25. License is null because git and the API are governed by GitHub terms and each repository carries its own license.

tools.name: PyGithub
tools.what: Python client for the GitHub REST API, used to script repository search, metadata and license lookups.
tools.when: Use it to avoid hand-writing HTTP calls in a collection script; skip it if gh or plain requests already covers your needs.
tools.connects: Takes a token and queries; hands repository metadata (stars, license, default branch) to the cloning and filtering steps.
tools.evidence: PyPI JSON (version 2.10.0, requires Python >=3.10) and GitHub API license field (LGPL-3.0), read 2026-11-25. Install name from PyPI project name; install line not copied from a README.

tools.name: Software Heritage archive, swh-graph and vault
tools.what: Universal archive of public source code; the swh.graph package downloads and queries its compressed graph locally, and the vault service cooks archived directories and revisions into downloadable bundles.
tools.when: Reach for it when you need provenance at scale or the exact archived state of a repository; for a few repositories git clone is simpler.
tools.connects: Takes SWHIDs or origin URLs; hands directory and revision contents with archive identifiers to deduplication and license steps.
tools.evidence: swh-graph quickstart (pip install swh.graph; swh graph download and grpc-serve commands) and swh-vault docs (cookers directory, git_bare, revision_flat, revision_gitfast) read 2026-11-25; PyPI JSON for swh.graph; GPL-3.0 from swh-graph GitHub API and PyPI classifier. Scale is a judgment (full graph size not checked). The documentation host returned HTTP 403 to a scripted browser user agent and pointed to the Software Heritage users ethical charter, so follow it for bulk access.

tools.name: Hugging Face datasets (streaming)
tools.what: Loads a Hub dataset lazily with load_dataset(..., streaming=True), so records are read without downloading the whole set.
tools.when: Use it to inspect or sample large public code datasets before committing disk; for gated sets accept the terms and log in first, and do not use it as a substitute for a pinned local copy in a final training run.
tools.connects: Takes a Hub dataset id; hands an iterable of records to filtering, dedup or a trainer.
tools.evidence: datasets README install line and the Stream docs page (streaming=True in load_dataset) read 2026-11-25; PyPI JSON requires Python >=3.10; license from GitHub API. The earlier snippet hf-datasets-streaming was run locally with datasets 4.5.0.

tools.name: GH Archive
tools.license: MIT (repository code); archive content may include third-party rights

latest_release.note: hourly data files, not a versioned package; repository has no release

tools.what: Hourly JSON archives of public GitHub timeline events (pushes, issues, pull requests), fetched over HTTP or queried in BigQuery.
tools.when: Use it to find which repositories and issues were active, or to build issue and pull-request signals; it holds events, not file contents, so you still need git or Software Heritage for code.
tools.connects: Takes a date range; hands event records (repository, actor, payload) to repository selection and issue-patch pairing.
tools.evidence: gharchive.org home page (example wget URLs, BigQuery mention) and the repository README (MIT code license; dataset may include third-party rights) read 2026-11-25.

tools.name: bigcode-dataset

latest_release.note: no GitHub release object; latest push 2024-08-15

tools.what: The BigCode project's code for building The Stack: language-to-extension selection, filters, PII handling, decontamination, and conversion scripts for notebooks, issues and commits.
tools.when: Read and adapt it when you want the reference recipe for a StarCoder-style dataset; do not expect a packaged library, because it is a set of scripts.
tools.connects: Takes raw repository files; hands filtered, decontaminated, redacted records to tokenization.
tools.evidence: Repository README contents list (language_selection, pii, decontamination, preprocessing) read 2026-11-25; license and last push (2024-08-15) from the GitHub API. No PyPI package exists (404).

tools.name: datatrove
tools.what: Pipeline library of readers, filters, MinHash deduplication, tokenization and writers that runs on local, Slurm or Ray executors.
tools.when: Use it to run the whole processing chain on many cores or a cluster (check its MinHash shingling on code, since the defaults are tuned for prose), and use datasets map/filter for a one-off script on a small set.
tools.connects: Takes jsonl or parquet shards from collection; hands deduplicated, filtered shards or tokenized files to training.
tools.install: uv sync   # from a clone of the repository; README requires Python 3.11+
tools.evidence: README installation section (Python 3.11+, uv sync, extras io, processing, s3, all) and PyPI JSON (requires_python >=3.10, so the README is the stricter statement) read 2026-11-25; license from PyPI and GitHub API.

tools.name: text-dedup
tools.what: Collection of ready-to-run deduplication scripts (MinHash, suffix array, Bloom filter and others) for text datasets.
tools.when: Reach for it when you want a tested near-duplicate script for a single machine; for cluster-scale runs use datatrove, and note it needs Python 3.12 or newer.
tools.connects: Takes a Hugging Face or local dataset; hands a deduplicated dataset to the next filter or the tokenizer.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/ChenghaoMou/text-dedup && cd text-dedup && uv sync
tools.evidence: README (Python 3.12+ badge, install via clone and uv sync) and PyPI JSON (version 0.4.1, requires >=3.12,<4.0) read 2026-11-25; license from GitHub API. Feature list beyond the README summary not checked.

tools.name: datasketch
tools.what: Python library implementing MinHash, MinHash LSH and related probabilistic sketches for near-duplicate search.
tools.when: Use it as a building block when you write your own code-aware dedup (for example shingling on tokens rather than words); use a ready pipeline if you just want results.
tools.connects: Takes token or shingle sets per file; hands duplicate clusters to a filter that keeps one file per cluster.
tools.evidence: README install line (pip install datasketch) and PyPI JSON (version 2.0.0, requires >=3.9, MIT) read 2026-11-25.

tools.name: py-tree-sitter (tree-sitter)
tools.what: Python bindings to the tree-sitter incremental parser, giving concrete syntax trees for code in many languages.
tools.when: Use it to drop files that do not parse, split code at function boundaries, or detect language; it does not run or type-check code.
tools.connects: Takes source files from collection; hands trees, spans and parse-success flags to filters and to formatting.
tools.install: pip install tree-sitter && pip install tree-sitter-python
tools.evidence: py-tree-sitter README installation section (pip install tree-sitter; language grammars installed as separate wheels, example tree-sitter-python) and PyPI JSON (version 0.27.0, requires >=3.11) read 2026-11-25.

tools.name: BigCode PII pipeline and StarPII
tools.license: Apache-2.0 (pipeline code); StarPII model card declares no license field and is gated

latest_release.note: no GitHub release object; latest push 2024-08-15

tools.what: Detects and redacts names, emails, IP addresses, passwords and keys in code datasets, using regexes plus detect-secrets (regex route) or the StarPII NER model.
tools.when: Use it before publishing or training on scraped code; treat its output as risk reduction, not proof of removal, because the README reports its own evaluation limits and the NER route needs GPUs.
tools.connects: Takes filtered code records; hands the same records with PII replaced by placeholders and extra columns of what was found.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/bigcode-project/bigcode-dataset.git && cd bigcode-dataset/pii && pip install -r requirements.txt
tools.evidence: pii/README.md (NER approach with StarPII, regex approach with detect-secrets, pip install -r requirements.txt, example main.py command, 800 GB in 800 A100 GPU-hours for StarCoderData) and Hugging Face API for bigcode/starpii (gated: auto, no license field) read 2026-11-25. Repository has no release object.

tools.name: detect-secrets
tools.what: Scans files for high-entropy strings and known secret patterns and writes a baseline of findings.
tools.when: Use it for a fast secret pass over code files; pair it with a second scanner because each has different false negatives, and its last release is from 2024.
tools.connects: Takes file contents; hands a findings list that a redaction step replaces or that drops the file.
tools.evidence: README (pip install detect-secrets; detect-secrets scan command) and PyPI JSON (version 1.5.0 released 2024-05-06) read 2026-11-25; the BigCode PII README names it as the key detector in its regex route.

tools.name: Gitleaks
tools.what: Detects secrets such as passwords, API keys and tokens in git repositories, files and stdin.
tools.when: Use it on whole cloned repositories, including git history, before files are flattened into a dataset; a Go binary, so it is not a Python library call.
tools.connects: Takes a repository or directory from collection; hands a findings report used to drop or redact files.
tools.install: brew install gitleaks   # or: docker pull ghcr.io/gitleaks/gitleaks:latest
tools.evidence: README install section (Homebrew, Docker, Go, release binaries) and GitHub releases API (v8.30.1, 2026-03-21) read 2026-11-25.

tools.name: ScanCode Toolkit
tools.license: Apache-2.0 AND CC-BY-4.0 (software Apache-2.0, data CC-BY-4.0)
tools.what: Scans files for licenses, copyrights and package metadata and reports SPDX-style license expressions.
tools.when: Use it for the license review that decides whether a file may enter the corpus; it is slow on large trees, and the pip route has no ARM wheels for some dependencies (see the Apple silicon note in its docs).
tools.connects: Takes cloned repositories; hands per-file license findings that a filter turns into allow and deny lists.
tools.evidence: ScanCode pip installation page (create venv, pip install scancode-toolkit, note on ARM chips), NOTICE file (SPDX Apache-2.0 AND CC-BY-4.0) and PyPI JSON (version 32.5.0, requires >=3.10) read 2026-11-25.

tools.name: go-license-detector
tools.what: Go tool that detects the license of a project directory by matching root license files to SPDX texts.
tools.when: Use it for a fast repository-level license label; it is unmaintained (last push 2023-06-09) and only reads project-level files, so prefer ScanCode when file-level answers matter.
tools.connects: Takes a cloned repository; hands one SPDX label with a confidence per repository.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/src-d/go-license-detector && cd go-license-detector && go build -v gopkg.in/src-d/go-license-detector.v3/cmd/license-detector
tools.evidence: README (algorithm: root license files, SPDX normalization; installation uses go mod download and go build; license Apache 2.0 per LICENSE.md) and GitHub API (last push 2023-06-09, latest release v3.1.0 2020-02-19) read 2026-11-25. Marked experimental because the project is dormant, not because the method is untested.

tools.name: Hugging Face datasets (map and filter)
tools.what: Applies a Python function to every record (Dataset.map) or keeps records that satisfy a predicate (Dataset.filter), with multiprocessing and on-disk caching.
tools.when: Use it for formatting, simple heuristics and prompt/completion construction on one machine; for global dedup or cluster scale, use datatrove.
tools.connects: Takes a loaded or streamed dataset; hands a dataset in the exact columns a trainer expects.
tools.evidence: Hugging Face datasets docs page 'process' (map and filter present) and README install line read 2026-11-25; the earlier snippet trl-sft-python uses map to build prompt/completion columns.

tools.name: Hugging Face tokenizers
tools.what: Fast Rust tokenizer library with Python bindings for training and running BPE, WordPiece and Unigram tokenizers.
tools.when: Use it to train a new code tokenizer or to load any tokenizer.json; for an existing model, load the model's own tokenizer instead.
tools.connects: Takes raw text or code from processing; hands token ids (or a trained tokenizer.json) to training.
tools.evidence: README install section (shows pip install --pre tokenizers; a stable 0.23.3 release is on PyPI, so the plain command is used) and PyPI JSON (requires >=3.10) read 2026-11-25.

tools.name: tiktoken
tools.what: Fast BPE tokenizer library that ships OpenAI's encodings and lets you define your own.
tools.when: Use it to count tokens for OpenAI-style models or to reuse their encodings; it is not the tokenizer for most open code models.
tools.connects: Takes text; hands token ids or token counts for budgeting and packing.
tools.evidence: README (pip install tiktoken) and PyPI JSON (version 0.14.0, requires >=3.9, MIT) read 2026-11-25.

tools.name: SentencePiece
tools.what: Unsupervised text tokenizer and detokenizer (BPE and unigram) that trains directly on raw text.
tools.when: Use it when a base model or recipe requires a SentencePiece model file; for a new tokenizer, tokenizers is usually easier to integrate.
tools.connects: Takes raw text; hands a .model file and token ids to training.
tools.evidence: README (pip install sentencepiece) and PyPI JSON (version 0.2.3, requires >=3.10, Apache-2.0) read 2026-11-25.

tools.name: The model's own tokenizer (transformers AutoTokenizer)
tools.license: Apache-2.0 (library); each tokenizer inherits its model's license
tools.what: Loads the exact tokenizer, special tokens and chat template that ship with a base model, so training and inference agree.
tools.when: Always use it when fine-tuning an existing model, and for fill-in-the-middle use that model's own FIM tokens (<fim_prefix>, <fim_suffix>, <fim_middle>, <fim_pad> in StarCoder2; <|fim_prefix|>, <|fim_suffix|>, <|fim_middle|>, <|fim_pad|> in Qwen2.5-Coder) and never another family's.
tools.connects: Takes raw code; hands token ids with the right special tokens and masks to the trainer.
tools.evidence: tokenizer_config.json of bigcode/starcoder2-3b (added tokens <fim_prefix>, <fim_middle>, <fim_suffix>, <fim_pad>, <repo_name>, <file_sep>) and Qwen/Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B (<|fim_prefix|>, <|fim_middle|>, <|fim_suffix|>, <|fim_pad|>, <|repo_name|>, <|file_sep|>) fetched from Hugging Face 2026-11-25; PyPI JSON for transformers 5.24.1 (requires >=3.11). Model licenses from the Hub API: StarCoder2 bigcode-openrail-m, Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B apache-2.0.

tools.name: Transformers
tools.what: Library of model definitions, tokenizers and a Trainer class that nearly every open training framework builds on.
tools.when: Use it directly for a custom loop or small experiment; for SFT, DPO or GRPO prefer TRL, which wraps it.
tools.connects: Takes tokenized datasets and a base model id; hands checkpoints (safetensors) to evaluation and the Hub.
tools.evidence: README install line and PyPI JSON (version 5.24.1, requires Python >=3.11, huggingface-hub>=1.31.0, tokenizers>=0.23.1,<0.24) read 2026-11-25. The local environment (transformers 4.57.3) is older than the 5.x line.

tools.name: TRL
tools.what: Post-training library with SFTTrainer, DPOTrainer, GRPOTrainer and other trainers, plus a trl command line, built on Transformers.
tools.when: Reach for it first for a small SFT or GRPO run on one to a few GPUs; for large multi-node RL use verl, OpenRLHF or SkyRL.
tools.connects: Takes a Hub or local dataset in prompt/completion or chat format and a base model; hands a fine-tuned model or LoRA adapter to evaluation.
tools.evidence: TRL pyproject.toml on main (requires-python >=3.11; transformers>=4.56.2, accelerate>=1.11.0, datasets>=4.7.0, torch>=2.6.0; extras peft>=0.18.0, deepspeed>=0.18.6, harbor) and README (pip install trl; trl sft CLI) read 2026-11-25; PyPI JSON version 1.18.2. pip on local Python 3.9 lists trl only up to 0.24.0, which confirms the 3.11 floor.

tools.name: PEFT
tools.what: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning library (LoRA, QLoRA-style adapters and others) that trains small adapter weights on a frozen base model.
tools.when: Use it when memory is the constraint; do not use it when you need the full capacity of continued pretraining.
tools.connects: Takes a base model from Transformers; hands a small adapter that TRL trains and that you merge or load at evaluation time.
tools.evidence: README install line and PyPI JSON (version 0.22.0, requires Python >=3.11) read 2026-11-25; TRL's peft extra asks for peft>=0.18.0.

tools.name: Accelerate
tools.what: Launcher and thin wrapper that runs the same PyTorch script on one GPU, many GPUs, many nodes, DeepSpeed or FSDP.
tools.when: Use it to go from one GPU to several without rewriting the script; TRL's own docs launch with torchrun, which is an equal choice.
tools.connects: Takes a training script; hands a process group that the trainer uses and that writes checkpoints.
tools.evidence: README install line, launch tutorial (accelerate launch, --multi_gpu, --num_processes) and examples/slurm/submit_multigpu.sh read 2026-11-25; PyPI JSON version 1.16.0, requires Python >=3.11.

tools.name: DeepSpeed
tools.what: Training and inference library with ZeRO optimizer-state, gradient and parameter sharding and offloading.
tools.when: Use ZeRO when a model does not fit with plain data parallelism; FSDP is the alternative inside PyTorch.
tools.connects: Takes a JSON config and a script from Transformers or TRL; hands sharded checkpoints that you consolidate before evaluation.
tools.evidence: README install line and TRL's DeepSpeed integration page (pip install deepspeed; set deepspeed=<config.json> in SFTConfig; launch with torchrun) read 2026-11-25; PyPI JSON version 0.20.1 (no requires_python declared); license from GitHub API.

tools.name: Axolotl
tools.what: YAML-driven fine-tuning tool (axolotl train config.yml) for SFT, preference training and LoRA, with multi-GPU and multi-node support.
tools.when: Use it when you want a config file instead of code; it pins exact versions of torch, transformers, peft and trl, so keep it in its own environment.
tools.connects: Takes a YAML config naming a dataset and base model; hands checkpoints or adapters to evaluation.
tools.install: uv venv --python 3.12 && source .venv/bin/activate && uv pip install torch==2.14.0 torchvision && uv pip install axolotl[deepspeed]
tools.evidence: README quickstart (uv venv --python 3.12, torch==2.14.0, axolotl[deepspeed], axolotl train examples/llama-3/lora-1b.yml) and PyPI JSON (version 0.21.1, requires >=3.12; pins transformers==5.20.1, peft==0.21.2, trl==1.14.1, datasets==5.0.1) read 2026-11-25.

tools.name: LLaMA-Factory
tools.what: Fine-tuning framework with a CLI and web UI covering continued pretraining, SFT, reward modeling, PPO, DPO and others across many model families.
tools.when: Use it for config-driven or UI-driven runs without writing code; its pins (datasets<=4.0.0, peft<=0.18.1, accelerate<=1.11.0) clash with current TRL, so use a separate environment.
tools.connects: Takes a dataset_info entry and a YAML config; hands checkpoints or merged weights to evaluation.
tools.install: git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/hiyouga/LlamaFactory.git && cd LlamaFactory && pip install -e . && pip install -r requirements/metrics.txt
tools.evidence: README installation section and the llamafactory-cli train example (examples/train_lora/qwen3_lora_sft.yaml) read 2026-11-25; PyPI JSON for llamafactory 0.9.5 (2026-05-30, requires >=3.11) with the pins quoted above.

tools.name: Unsloth
tools.what: Training library with custom kernels for faster, lower-memory LoRA, QLoRA, full fine-tuning and GRPO on a single GPU, plus a local UI.
tools.when: Use it to fit a larger model on one consumer or workstation GPU; check its docs before relying on multi-GPU, which was not verified here.
tools.connects: Takes a Hub model and a prompt/completion dataset; hands adapters or merged weights (including GGUF) onward.
tools.install: uv venv unsloth_env --python 3.13 && source unsloth_env/bin/activate && uv pip install unsloth --torch-backend=auto
tools.evidence: README Unsloth Core install block (Linux, WSL) and feature line (LoRA, QLoRA, full fine tuning, pretraining, RL, GRPO, DPO, FP8) read 2026-11-25; PyPI JSON version 2026.11.11 (requires >=3.9,<3.15). GitHub release tags use a different scheme (v0.1.924-beta, 2026-11-24).

tools.name: torchtune
tools.what: PyTorch-native library of hackable fine-tuning recipes (SFT, distillation, DPO, PPO, GRPO) driven by YAML configs.
tools.when: Read it for clean reference recipes; do not start a new project on it, because its README states it is no longer actively maintained.
tools.connects: Takes a YAML config and a downloaded base model; hands checkpoints to evaluation.
tools.install: pip install torch torchvision torchao && pip install torchtune
tools.evidence: README banner (no longer actively maintained; development wound down in 2025) and install section, PyPI JSON (version 0.6.1 released 2025-04-07) read 2026-11-25.

tools.name: verl
tools.what: HybridFlow RL post-training framework that runs PPO, GRPO and related algorithms with FSDP or Megatron training and vLLM or SGLang rollouts on Ray.
tools.when: Use it for execution-based RL at multi-GPU or cluster scale with a custom reward function; for a first fine-tune use TRL.
tools.connects: Takes parquet prompts with ground truth and a reward function (which can call a sandbox); hands RL-trained checkpoints that you merge with verl.model_merger.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/verl-project/verl && cd verl   # no install step; prefix commands with: uv run --frozen --all-packages --extra vllm --extra fsdp
tools.evidence: Installation page (uv workflow, Linux, Python 3.12, extras vllm|sglang and fsdp|megatron) and quickstart (GSM8K PPO, needs a GPU with at least 24 GB) read 2026-11-25; PyPI JSON version 0.9.1 (requires >=3.10,<3.13, transformers>=5.5.3,<5.11). The catalog also lists this project as fw-verl under the old volcengine URL.

tools.name: OpenRLHF
tools.what: Ray, vLLM and DeepSpeed based framework for PPO, REINFORCE++, GRPO and RLOO training, plus SFT and reward-model training.
tools.when: Use it when you want a DeepSpeed-based RL stack with a Docker-first setup; it pins deepspeed==0.19.6 and flash-attn==2.8.3, so isolate it.
tools.connects: Takes prompt datasets and an optional reward function or agent; hands trained actor checkpoints to evaluation.
tools.install: pip install openrlhf[vllm]   # run inside nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:26.03-py3 as the README recommends
tools.evidence: README Installation section (docker run with nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:26.03-py3, pip install openrlhf[vllm]) and ray job submit example read 2026-11-25; PyPI JSON version 0.11.2 (requires >=3.10).

tools.name: SkyRL
tools.what: Modular full-stack RL library for LLMs with training backends, a gymnasium of tool-use environments and an agent layer, integrated with Harbor.
tools.when: Use it for multi-turn agent RL on real environments such as terminal or SWE tasks; it requires CUDA 13.0, so check your driver first.
tools.connects: Takes parquet prompts and an environment class; hands RL-trained checkpoints and trajectories to evaluation.
tools.evidence: Installation docs (CUDA 13.0, driver r580 or newer, uv, Docker image above, git clone https://github.com/novasky-ai/SkyRL.git) and quickstart (GRPO on GSM8K via uv run --isolated --extra fsdp -m skyrl.train.entrypoints.main_base) read 2026-11-25; PyPI JSON version 0.5.0 (requires >=3.12,<3.15). The catalog also lists this project as fw-skyrl under the old NovaSky-AI URL.

tools.name: vLLM
tools.what: High-throughput inference and serving engine (PagedAttention, continuous batching, OpenAI-compatible server) used to sample from the policy.
tools.when: Use it as the rollout and evaluation sampler; TRL, verl, OpenRLHF and SkyRL all call it, so match the version they pin.
tools.connects: Takes a model checkpoint; hands generated completions to a reward function, a sandbox or an evaluator.
tools.evidence: README install line and feature list, quickstart (Python 3.11 to 3.14, uv venv, vllm serve), and TRL's vLLM integration page (vllm serve in server mode) read 2026-11-25; PyPI JSON version 0.34.0.

tools.name: SGLang
tools.what: High-performance serving framework for language and multimodal models, used as an alternative rollout engine.
tools.when: Use it when your RL framework supports it as a rollout backend (verl lists sglang as an extra) or you prefer its serving features; vLLM is the more common default.
tools.connects: Takes a model checkpoint; hands completions to the same reward and evaluation steps as vLLM.
tools.install: uv pip install --prerelease=allow sglang   # or: docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:latest
tools.evidence: README install section (Docker image and uv command) and verl install page (extras vllm or sglang) read 2026-11-25; PyPI JSON version 0.5.23 (requires >=3.11).

tools.name: Weights & Biases
tools.what: Experiment tracker that logs metrics, configs, artifacts and system stats to a hosted or self-hosted dashboard.
tools.when: Use it for team dashboards and sweeps; it needs an account and API key, so choose Trackio or TensorBoard for a no-account local setup.
tools.connects: Takes metrics from the trainer (report_to=wandb) and eval scripts; hands run URLs and artifacts for comparing experiments.

tools.name: Docker (Moby)
tools.what: Container runtime that isolates processes with namespaces and cgroups on the host kernel; hardened flags (no network, read-only root, dropped capabilities, resource limits) tighten it.
tools.when: Use it as the default sandbox for tests and RL rewards on trusted-ish model output; for adversarial code add a stronger layer such as gVisor or a microVM, because the kernel is shared.
tools.connects: Takes a candidate program and tests mounted read-only; hands exit code, stdout and a timeout verdict back to the reward or evaluator.
tools.evidence: Docker Engine security page (namespaces and cgroups give isolation; intrinsic kernel security is listed as a review area) read 2026-11-25; the hardened command was run on Docker 29.1.3 on 2026-11-24 (see data/snippets.json docker-hardened-sandbox) with flags checked against docker/cli source. GitHub releases API: docker-v29.10.1, 2026-11-24. Install of the daemon is OS specific and not covered here; the hardened run command is in data/setups.json.

tools.name: gVisor
tools.what: Application kernel (runsc runtime) written in Go that intercepts a container's system calls so the program does not talk to the host kernel directly.
tools.when: Use it behind Docker or Kubernetes when you run untrusted code and want stronger isolation than plain containers; expect some syscall incompatibility and overhead.
tools.connects: Takes the same OCI container as Docker; hands the same result streams while the workload runs against gVisor's kernel.
tools.evidence: README and gvisor.dev home ('provides a strong layer of isolation between running applications and the host operating system'; runsc integrates with Docker and Kubernetes) read 2026-11-25; GitHub releases API: release-20261123.0. Install is null because the quick-start page (gvisor.dev/docs/user_guide/quick_start/docker/) was not read.

tools.name: Firecracker
tools.what: Virtual machine monitor that runs lightweight KVM microVMs for secure, multi-tenant, minimal-overhead execution.
tools.when: Use it when you run untrusted code at scale and need hardware-virtualization isolation; it needs KVM and your own orchestration, so most teams use it through a hosted service.
tools.connects: Takes a kernel image, root filesystem and a job; hands console output or files back through your guest agent.

tools.name: nsjail
tools.what: Linux process-isolation tool that combines namespaces, resource limits, read-only mounts and seccomp-bpf syscall filters in one command.
tools.when: Use it to wrap a single untrusted process with a syscall policy without a container runtime; it shares the host kernel and you write the policy.
tools.connects: Takes a command and a config or flags; hands the process exit status and output after limits are applied.

Build-from-source steps (apt dependencies, make, or docker build -t nsjail .) are from the README Installation section.
